conflict_topics: presence and visibility of alcohol in shared fridge
storage/location versus refrigeration needs for party drinks
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents provide clear, conversational reasons (D's disclosure, A's logistics constraint).
Proposals move from hypothetical (buy later) to practical (box/bags in fridge).
No needless repetition; turns are concise and on-topic.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent D disclosed being a recovering alcoholic and expressed that having large amounts of alcohol in the shared fridge is difficult for them. The group proposed several accommodations (buying just before the party — rejected as infeasible by Agent A; keeping drinks in Agent A's room — rejected due to refrigeration needs; hiding them in a box/bags at back of fridge — accepted by Agent D), but Agent A has not agreed to or enacted the remaining practical step (placing the drinks in a box/bags or otherwise altering storage). Therefore the substantive incompatibility (who will change storage behavior to avoid D seeing alcohol) remains unsettled.
position_change_notes: Agent D moved from passive concern ('that's a lot of alcohol') to explicit disclosure of a recovery condition, clarifying the substantive need ('I'm a recovering alcoholic...').
Agent C and B shifted from neutral to active problem-solving, proposing alternatives (buy later, keep in room, hide in box/bags).

Agent A has maintained a consistent position about practical constraints: drinks are already purchased, non-returnable, and need refrigeration; no concession or implementation promise by Agent A is recorded in the transcript.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 2–3: Agent B thanks Agent A and Agent A replies 'No problem. Hope it's enough for everyone.' No incompatible positions expressed.
Turn 4–5: Agent B says 'Should be fine.' Agent C asks Agent D if they're alright. No substantive disagreement yet.

Turn 6–7: Agent D expresses a concern: 'That's a lot of alcohol to have in the house.' This introduces a substantive incompatibility between having alcohol visible in the shared space and someone’s comfort/safety.

Turn 10–11: Agent D discloses 'I'm a recovering alcoholic... It's difficult for me to have that much sitting in the fridge.' This makes the conflict explicit between Agent D's need to avoid exposure and the presence of alcohol in the shared fridge.

Turn 12–13: Agent C proposes buying drinks just before the party to avoid alcohol in the house; Agent A replies 'I already bought all this. And the shop doesn't do returns.' The proposal conflicts with Agent A's stated facts, so the core incompatibility remains.

Turn 14–15: Agent C suggests 'can you keep it in your room until Saturday?'; Agent A counters 'It needs to be kept in the fridge... it has to be cold for the party.' A practical incompatibility about storage/location versus refrigeration persists.

Turn 16–17: Agent B proposes a compromise: 'put them in a cooler box, or just some black plastic bags, at the back of the fridge' to reduce visibility. This softens the conflict but does not yet resolve who will act or whether that satisfies all constraints.

Turn 18–19: Agent D accepts the proposed accommodation: 'Yeah, I think that would help... As long as I don't have to see it right there when I open the door.' Agent C asks Agent A to implement it, but Agent A has not yet agreed, so a small unresolved practical issue remains (who will move/pack the drinks).

substantive_insights: The conflict is factual/practical (who can store the drinks and where) rather than purely normative; A's purchases and refrigeration needs constrain options.
Disclosure of a personal vulnerability (recovering alcoholism) shifted the discussion from general discomfort to an accommodation problem.
Proposed accommodation (concealment at back of fridge) is acceptable to the person with the vulnerability but depends on Agent A's agreement/implementation.
